extracted.intended_audience: aspiring essayists, moralists, and creative writers interested in character, taste, and rhetorical technique
extracted.subtask_short: writing moral essays and character sketches
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing moral/character essays and short pieces that use anecdote, allegory, classical allusion, and vivid description to reveal vice and virtue. Emphasises portrayal of character by action/motion, use of contrasts, and the rhetorical use of nature and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant Fellow — charm masking vice
rubrics_metrics.description: A very pleasant Fellow shall turn your good Name to a Jest, make your Character contemptible, debauch your Wife or Daughter, and yet be received by the rest of the World with Welcome where-ever he appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray 'pleasant' characters as superficially attractive but morally dangerous: attentive chiefly to their own satisfactions, with little compassion, capable of purchasing their own pleasures at the expense of giving pain to others. Use this type as a foil — their amiability may hide ill qualities and lead to social harm and private ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride and susceptibility to flatterers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is no one Passion which all Mankind so naturally give into as Pride, nor any other Passion which appears in such different Disguises... It is this Passion alone, when misapplyed, that lays us so open to Flatterers; and he who can agreeably condescend to sooth our Humour or Temper, finds always an open Avenue to our Soul; especially if the Flatterer happen to be our Superior.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting characters, show how pride (in many disguises) makes them vulnerable to flattery. Use examples or scenes where flattering speech or familiar condescension opens trust or power to manipulation, particularly in relationships of superiority/subordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anecdote/historical example to illustrate moral points
rubrics_metrics.description: The story of King Charles II and the mayor (who caught him by the hand and cried 'Sir, You shall stay and take t'other Bottle') is used to show how a monarch's familiarity and gaiety disarmed jealousy and won public favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid, specific anecdotes (historical or invented) to embody abstract moral claims. A short, concrete episode can make a general statement memorable and persuasive; keep the detail that shows character and consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of nature in art (dancing as example)
rubrics_metrics.description: As all Art is an Imitation of Nature... The Business of Dancing is to display Beauty, and for that Reason all Distortions and Mimickries, as such, are what raise Aversion instead of Pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In describing or composing art (dance, movement, voice, etc.), insist that performance imitate natural grace appropriate to the character. Avoid grotesque distortions or mere novelty; motions should fit the character being represented and proceed from truth rather than gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion and performance reveal character
rubrics_metrics.description: No one ever was a good Dancer, that had not a good Understanding. Motion, and change of Posture and Aspect, has an Effect no less surprising... when she Dances [Mariamne] all the latent good Qualities which appeared in her Countenance are set forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public performance or bodily behaviour (dance, manner, posture) as a device to reveal inner qualities. Small gestures (a father's nod, a modest look) can credibly dramatise dignity, virtue, or folly; make physical action do the showing rather than telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory to teach about wealth, virtue, and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plutus allegory: Plutus (the god of riches) blind as to distribution, Poverty pleading her cause, later reclaiming sight and enriching the pious and just while taking wealth from the impious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use allegory to encapsulate moral lessons about social conditions (wealth/poverty, vice/virtue). A personified, narrative allegory can render abstract tendencies (e.g., 'Riches corrupt the morals of those who possessed them') perceptible and memorable; include ironic or comic incidents to make the point lively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrasts and the emblem of scales to reveal intrinsic value
rubrics_metrics.description: In a vision a pair of Golden Scales weighed 'the Value of every thing that is in Esteem among Men.' Wisdom vs Riches, Vanity counterpoised to Titles and Honours, and other balances reveal true worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure pieces around contrasts and balancing metaphors to show how apparent value differs from intrinsic worth. Try juxtaposing pairs (wisdom/riches, learning/natural_parts, faith/morality) and use a single emblem (e.g., scales) to dramatise judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid valuing by appearances; regulate esteem by intrinsic worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve not to despise or value any Things for their Appearances, but to regulate my Esteem and Passions towards them according to their real and intrinsick Value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the moral of your piece explicit through action and reflection: expose false esteem (vanity, titles) and encourage readers to measure characters and goods by intrinsic qualities. Use examples and fables to show the cost of superficial valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith strengthened by practice and retreat, not by perpetual controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who delight in reading Books of Controversie... do very seldom arrive at a fixed and settled Habit [of faith]. There is nothing which strengthens Faith more than Morality... habitual Adoration... frequent Retirement from the World, accompanied with religious Meditation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating belief or conviction in fiction/essay, show that faith is rooted in lived morality, devotion, and retreat into nature/solitude rather than endless disputation. Character arcs should foreground practice and experiential signs of conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cosmic/pastoral imagery to declare the divine
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spacious Firmament... Their great Original proclaim... The Sun... publishes to every Land The Work of an Almighty Hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ large-scale natural imagery (firmament, sun, stars, seasons) and personification to make theological or existential claims feel grand and persuasive. Poems or lyrical passages can 'let Nature speak' and serve as a confirmatory witness to a theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of condition favors wisdom; extremes corrupt
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle Condition seems to be the most advantageously situated for the gaining of Wisdom... Poverty is apt to betray a Man into Envy, Riches into Arrogance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constructing social types, use socioeconomic position to explain tendencies: show how poverty and riches produce different vices and virtues, and use a 'middle condition' as a suitable site for balanced, reflective characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining qualities produces a multiplicative effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural Parts weighed much heavier when Learning was in the same Scale with it... Faith and Morality... received a thousand times more additional Weight from its Conjunction with the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing characters or arguments, pair complementary qualities (e.g., intellect + learning, faith + morality) to produce a compounded impression of worth. Dramatically demonstrate synergies rather than treating traits in isolation.
